blocks.text: They saw it first in a letter. Then in a hangar of pale stone, the same one where a woman had promised to accept the no of a quayside. Andrés, mending the net, felt the apparatus the way you feel a new engine: not entirely hostile, not entirely of home. It was tall, made of a matt metal, with two arches that weren't a door and looked like one. On the floor, a circle. In the air, a smell of filters and of a dry storm, like Selene Norte, like the seedbed's workshop.

blocks.text: The clone was there, and the woman from the hangar, and some of her people, and a technician who wasn't from Nexum or had stopped being so. On a table, a cup. Not the cracked one from Lo Pagán: an ordinary earthenware cup, already with a hairline crack, honest.

blocks.text: “This first,” said the one who searches, and Andrés heard it with his fingers on the rope. “If the cup arrives and it's this cup, we'll talk about a body. If a different one arrives, we go home and leave the phrase to the brochures.”

blocks.text: The cup was placed in the circle. The machine didn't roar. It made, barely, a denser silence. The earthenware ceased to be there. No visible dust remained in the air: what remained, the technician said afterwards, was a record, an order, a weight that hadn't evaporated but had been named. Nothing is lost, they kept saying. Andrés, in the courtyard, felt the emptiness on that table the way you probe with your tongue for a tooth that's no longer there.

blocks.text: On the other side (in a second machine, a twin, installed not in Madrid but, against Helena's wishes and not entirely against Andrés's, in a discreet warehouse near El Estacio, brought in at night, with no pearl-grey van at the door of the house) the cup was put together. Lía was a witness. So was Aya. The earthenware was there. So was the hairline crack. The weight was the same, or so close that a kitchen scale could find nothing missing. Lía didn't touch it straight away. She looked at it the way you look at a fruit that might come from a portrait.

blocks.text: “May I?” she asked, out of habit, and nobody understood whether she was asking the cup or them. She picked it up. It was cold. To the finger, it was made of earthenware. Not of an idea.

blocks.text: “It's the same one,” said Aya, and in her voice there was wonder and a reservation. “Or it's so much the same one that this house has no instrument for saying it isn't.”

blocks.text: Lía took it to the kitchen in Lo Pagán and put it beside the cracked one, and the two looked like sisters: one had crossed a sky, the other had never left the sink.

blocks.text: That afternoon the technician, through the bridge and on a screen, explained what he could explain without turning it into a miracle: that a body, or a cup, can be described as an order; that this order can, if the machine gets it right, be taken apart and assembled; that energy is neither created nor destroyed, it only changes shape; that the original, here, doesn't remain, because if it did there would be two, and the machine, because of a limitation the technician called “one of principle”, doesn't duplicate. It either assembles or it doesn't. It doesn't copy.

blocks.text: Andrés kept that limitation the way you keep a mooring line: it doesn't duplicate. So it wasn't the valley of the same face. So it was something else, graver and cleaner.

blocks.text: “If I crossed,” he said on the doorstep that night, “this body would stop being in this chair. You, Aya, would be left for a while with an empty chair. Then, if the other machine got it right, I'd be in a hangar, or he'd be here, and this chair would have a weight in it again. Would you wait for me in the emptiness?”

Then, if the other machine got it right, I'd be in a hangar, or he'd be here, and this chair would have a weight in it again. Would you wait for me in the emptiness?”

blocks.text: Aya thought about it, which was her way of not filling with words what had no name yet.
blocks.html: Aya thought about it, which was her way of not filling with words what had no name yet.

blocks.text: “I'd wait for you the way I waited for the boat in the levante,” she said. “Without notifying Madrid. With the coffee made again. But don't ask me not to feel, during that while, that you've come to an end. Even if the phrase says nothing is lost. In this house, a while of absence is also something that exists.”

blocks.text: Lía set the cup that had crossed on the table, not as an altar but as a piece of evidence.
blocks.html: Lía set the cup that had crossed on the table, not as an altar but as a piece of evidence.

blocks.text: “A cup doesn't ask whether it's the same,” she said. “A man does. When we send someone across, I'll be beside the machine here, and I'll ask. If the machine doesn't allow questions, it isn't a shore: it's an appliance. And appliances, as we know, want an owner.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked:

blocks.text: *If a cup arrives with its crack, has the crack travelled, or has it been written again? And if one day a man arrives with his memory, who can sign to say that the memory hasn't been written again as well?*

blocks.text: MAY, beside her, the fact:
blocks.html: MAY, beside her, the fact:

blocks.text: *A cup has been taken apart in a hangar and put together near El Estacio. The original has not remained on the table over there. The weight and the crack match. It is claimed that the machine does not duplicate. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: Before sleeping, Andrés touched both cups, the one that had crossed and the one that hadn't. Both sounded like earthenware. One, however, left on his finger a warehouse coldness, a not-having-always-been-here. It wasn't proof of falseness. It was proof of a journey. And he, who had received worlds without setting foot on them, understood that this phrase, “nothing is lost”, was very soon going to ask of him something the letters never asked: his whole body, the body of this shore, placed in a circle, and the faith, or the doubt, that what is put back together on the other side still truly tastes of coffee.

blocks.text: In the morning, Lía took the cup that had crossed to the plot, filled it with tap water, Lo Pagán water, and left it in the sun, like a windowsill. Not to see whether it would ripen, since a cup doesn't ripen, but to see whether this shore's day would recognise it. A humanoid from the gardens glanced at it sideways and didn't ask: in 2060, and in the years after, people had seen everything, except this. Lía told it, all the same, the minimal truth:

blocks.text: “It came from a sky. It's still a cup. If one day people come, I'll offer them water in it, if they ask for it. Not before.”

blocks.text: Iago, who had heard the end of it, shook his head, not entirely convinced, not entirely against. He sat down and asked for neither eternity nor transfer. He asked only to be told if the machine came any closer to the house, so he wouldn't trip over it when he brought the figs. It was the request of a man of the soil, and Lía kept it the way you keep a good knot.

blocks.text: Andrés, as he went out to fish, left the cup that had crossed where it was, in the kitchen, and the usual cup too. Two shores, now, in a single sink. The Mar Menor was still. He was not, entirely.
